A Private Journey or a Big-Brand River Cruise Package? What the Difference Buys

A fair comparison of a private Egypt journey and a big-brand river cruise package: group size, guides, timing, boats, price and how to compare two quotes

17 November 2026 · 13 minute read

By Islam Hussein, Sillage Égypte journey designer. Last updated: November 2026.

The quick answer

A river cruise package buys predictability: one payment, a shared ship, a fixed excursion schedule and a local guide at each port. A private journey buys control: your own car, a boat chosen for the journey where the river belongs in it, and one certified Egyptologist from the first day to the last, with hours chosen for light and quiet rather than coach arrivals. Take the package for amenities and certainty; take the private journey for timing, depth and room to change the plan.

Price band Sillage journeys €2,190 to €11,650 per person, for two or more travellers, in luxury hotels (Christmas & New Year on the Nile from €9,999) Quoted per person by cabin category; check whether flights sit inside the figure

Every autumn our inbox fills with the same careful sentence: "We have found a river cruise package with a well-known line, but we keep reading about private journeys as an alternative. Which should we choose?" The honest answer: both are good products for different travellers, often at similar money. This post compares them properly (group size, guides, timing, boats, flexibility and price) and ends with a method for comparing any two quotes you are holding. Sillage Égypte (sillage-egypte.com), the private Egypt journey designer, designs the private kind, so we write as the interested party, and will try to earn your trust by being fair to the other side. If a big-brand package is the right answer for you, this post should leave you certain of it.

The short answer

A package buys predictability on a shared ship and schedule; a private journey buys control of timing, one guide throughout and visits outside the crowded hours. Everything else in this comparison follows from that one difference.

  • Travellers who want the pool, the sun deck and the evening show: take the package, without apology. Amenity at that scale is a genuine skill, and private journeys simply do not offer it.
  • First-time visitors who find certainty restful: take the package. Knowing exactly what Tuesday holds is worth real money on a first Egypt trip.
  • Anyone who has seen Egypt from a coach column and vowed never again: go private. You already know precisely what a fixed excursion schedule costs you.
  • Photographers and the crowd-averse: go private. Timing is the Egyptologist's craft, and the Valley of the Kings at opening is a different site from the same tombs at eleven.
  • Families with young children: usually the package: pool, playmates, per-cabin pricing, three or four nights. Families spanning three generations: often private: one pace that bends around the oldest and the youngest at once.
  • Solo travellers watching the arithmetic: the package. A ship will sell you one cabin; a Sillage journey is priced per person for two or more travellers, and a solo price comes in the proposal.
  • Travellers for whom "tailor-made" is a promise rather than a chore: private. The refining together is the product.

Who a package suits

A river cruise package suits travellers who value predictability above control, and predictability is a real good, not a consolation prize. One payment goes to one company, and the whole chain (flights, transfers, the ship, the excursion programme) becomes that company's problem rather than yours. In Britain and the EU, a proper package also carries statutory financial protection that separately booked parts do not (UK Package Travel Regulations 2018; EU Directive 2015/2302). For many travellers, that wrap is precisely what a holiday is for.

The ship itself is the other half of the case. A pool on the sun deck, a spa, a gym, shows in the lounge, dinner done properly at scale: amenity afloat is a genuine craft, and the better lines do it very well. The programme suits first-timers (there is real comfort in knowing that Tuesday is Edfu, whatever Edfu turns out to be) and it suits sociable travellers, families with young children, and anyone who measures a day by what is arranged rather than what is possible. Many lines put licensed Egyptologists on their excursions.

What the package cannot sell you is the clock. The ship's arrival slots set the hours; the excursion programme sets the pace; the convoy, the shared rhythm of coaches and crowds that moves Egypt's mass tourism, is simply the package's native weather. No shame in any of it. But the tombs at eleven are not the tombs at seven, and no cabin category changes that.

Who a private journey suits

A private journey suits travellers who care most about when, how deeply and with whom they see Egypt: the three things a shared schedule cannot sell. This is the bespoke end of Egyptian travel, and what it actually changes is three things: the guide, the clock and the boat. Sillage journeys are private throughout (your own car, a boat chosen for the journey where the river belongs in it, no scheduled departures, no shared groups) and every published journey, the full list is here, is a starting point tailored entirely to the people travelling.

One guide, first day to last, is the difference travellers most underestimate. A certified Egyptologist who travels with you from Cairo to Aswan knows by day three what questions you ask, which walls you linger at and which specialism to lend them: New Kingdom hieroglyphs, Nubian history, Islamic Cairo. Excursion guides meet a new group each morning; your Egyptologist is someone who can read the walls rather than recite a script, and by the second week is reading them for you. The clock is the second difference: chosen hours rather than fixed hours, which in practice means the hours our Egyptologists time all season.

  • The Valley of the Kings opens at 6 a.m. (Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities). The first quiet hour belongs to whoever is there at opening; by mid-morning the coaches own the air.
  • Edfu's Temple of Horus, among the best-preserved temples in Egypt, opens at 7 a.m. and is nearly yours before eight; afterwards, the calèche carriages that meet the ships arrive.
  • At Kom Ombo, the double temple of Sobek and Horus, a ship's mooring slot sets your hour; on a private journey the hour is part of the plan.
  • The standard Valley of the Kings ticket covers three tombs, and the tombs of Seti I (KV17), Tutankhamun and Ramesses VI (KV9) are separate tickets (Trvlogue; tombs also close in rotation for conservation). Nefertari's tomb in the Valley of the Queens has been reported closed since March 2024, with no reopening date (Explore Ena). Knowing which tombs a quote includes is knowing the quote.

The boat is the third difference. On The Complete Egypt it is a dahabiya, a shallow-draught traditional Nile sailing boat with a handful of cabins and a full crew, chartered whole for your party, not a cabin on a shared deck. The Nile & the Red Sea and Beyond the Nile use the Oberoi Zahra, a luxury cruiser, as part of the private journey. Five nights sailing Esna to Aswan on The Complete Egypt, mooring at Gebel el-Silsila and El-Kab where the deep-draught ships cannot tie up, is a different river from the same water shared with strangers.

Honest counsel about who should not book one. A private journey is wrong for travellers who measure comfort in amenities: on a dahabiya there is no pool, no spa, no gala night. It is wrong for anyone who finds choosing tiring: the refining is a pleasure for some travellers and homework for others, and you should know which you are before you begin. And a party of one watching the arithmetic will usually find the per-cabin price of a package wins, and fairly. One more honest limit: special access, such as a private Giza plateau or a tomb beyond the standard ticket, depends on permission; we request each permission and its cost on booking and confirm them in writing before the balance is due. We never promise a permit; if it is declined you hear from us and the journey is reshaped. If you are still matching the shape of journey to your party, our comparison of the journeys walks through that question.

How to compare two quotes fairly

Comparing two Egypt quotes is an accounting exercise before it is a travel decision: per person, per day, with everything inside and outside each figure on the table. Seven steps, in order.

  1. Divide by the right unit. A package is priced per person, usually on two sharing, with any single supplement separate. A Sillage journey is priced per person for two or more travellers; run the division at your actual party size, and check what each quote assumes about it.
  2. Ask what sits inside each figure. International flights sit outside Sillage journeys and sometimes inside a package's. Domestic flights within Egypt and the Egyptian entry visa are inside ours; ask the same of the package. Entrance fees, and which tombs they cover, should be named in both. Gratuities sit outside ours, and often outside a package's too; comprehensive travel insurance is a condition of booking with Sillage.
  3. Count the guides. One Egyptologist throughout, or a sequence of port guides? Ask both quotes who meets you at the airport, a private welcome inside the terminal or a driver with a sign, and whether you will see that person again.
  4. Ask the time-of-day question. "What time will we be at the Valley of the Kings?" One quote will answer "morning excursion"; the other "at opening". Both answers are true. They are not the same morning.
  5. Check what is named. Hotels by name, the boat by name, the guide by name, or "a five-star Nile cruiser or similar". A quote that names nothing is telling you something.
  6. Read the terms together. Deposit size, balance date, cancellation scale, what happens to the price after confirmation. With Sillage: a 25% non-refundable deposit secures the booking, the balance is due 60 days before arrival, bookings inside 60 days are paid in full, and the price is fixed once confirmed in writing, except for government action, taxes and fees, or significant currency changes. Cancelling with 60 or more days' notice forfeits the deposit only; 59 to 30 days costs 50%, 29 to 15 days 75%, and 14 days or fewer 100% (our booking terms).
  7. Test the conversation. Before any money moves, send each side one specific question (a date, a tomb, an hour) and watch what comes back. An enquiry with Sillage is free, and a named journey designer replies within 24 hours; so should any company worth its quote.

For scale, one honest example: The Complete Egypt is a 13-day private journey with five nights on a private dahabiya from Esna to Aswan, a certified Egyptologist throughout, private cars and luxury hotels, from €7,500 per person for two or more travellers, with domestic flights and the visa included. Set any package quote beside it and run the seven steps; the arithmetic will tell you more than either brochure.

FAQ

Should I book a well-known river cruise line's Egypt package or a private tour? Book the package if predictability, onboard amenities and a per-person price matter most to you; book the private journey if the hours you stand at the monuments, one guide throughout and room to change the plan matter most. Neither answer is superior: the two products simply optimise for different holidays.

Is a private Egypt tour better than a package? Better at some things, honestly not at others. Private travel wins on timing, depth and flexibility; the package wins on predictability, amenities and per-person cost. "Better" only means better for the traveller you are: the crowd-averse photographer and the family that lives for the pool should usually answer differently.

How much more does a private journey cost? Sillage journeys run from €2,190 to €11,650 per person depending on length and style (Christmas & New Year on the Nile from €9,999), and packages are usually lower per person. The headline figures matter less than what sits inside them: run the seven steps in the quotes section on both, and the real gap will show itself.

Can I have a private guide while sailing on a big cruise ship? Partially. Some lines and their agents can arrange private excursions at the ports, but the ship's arrival slots still set the clock. For a river week that is private all the way through, the alternative is a dahabiya chartered whole for your party.

What if I actually want the pool and the gala night? Take the package, with our blessing. Wanting a ship's amenity inventory is not a lesser form of travel, and no private journey will conjure a pool beside a temple. Choosing the product that matches your appetite is the point: we keep a whole piece on talking people out of the wrong trip.

Is a private journey harder to book than a package? No, but it is a different shape of booking. You describe the trip; a named journey designer replies within 24 hours with a private proposal; you refine it together, free and without obligation. A 25% non-refundable deposit then secures the journey, with the balance due 60 days before arrival.

Which suits a family with children? Young children usually suit the package: pool, playmates, three- or four-night sailings, per-cabin pricing. Families with older children, or three generations travelling together, often suit a private journey, where one pace bends around tired legs, teenagers and grandparents' knees.

The takeaway

A package buys a well-run Egypt on a shared clock; a private journey buys Egypt on yours: one guide who stays, hours chosen for light and quiet, a boat chosen for the journey where the river belongs in it. Both are legitimate answers, and only you know which difference you would actually use.
